newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli fights government over East Jerusalem.
newsitem.headline: Israeli fights government over East Jerusalem.

text.p: Israeli developer David Myr owned half the land confiscated by his government for a Jewish neighbourhood in Arab East Jerusalem.

Myr, who wanted to build for Jews himself on the site, says the Palestinian Authority would not have objected to his plans which could have been implemented, he believes, without endangering the Middle East peace process.
"They know me and I met with them and they said 'We see that you are not a troublemaker and we can agree with you'," he said.
"The problem is in this case or in any case people confuse two things: ownership and who will have power over this region."

PLO official Ziad Abu Zayyad, who deals with Jerusalem affairs, told Reuters he knew Myr, wished him well in court cases against Israel, and said if any were successful they could "talk then...But I don't say what the outcome would be".

Myr, 55, spoke to Reuters at his office tucked in a shady West Jerusalem suburb surrounded by scale models of his plans for the hill Israelis call Har Homa and Palestinians call Jabal Abu Ghneim. Israel captured it in the 1967 Middle East war.
Myr bought the land from Arabs in 1970.
He still has three cases pending against the confiscation before Israel's High Court, the last initiated in June 1996.
On Wednesday, Israel's High Court ordered the attorney general to explain within 10 days why it should not issue an interim injunction requested by Myr against government plans.
Myr said it made no difference to him who ruled, he wanted to build the luxury neighbourhood complete with a golf course he has planned for the last 25 years.
"They (Israel) are creating problems with all the nations and it is not necessary...the Arabs can build on their land and the Jews can build on our land and we will not create any problem," he said.
Israel confiscated 192 hectares at Har Homa in 1992 under the previous Labour government. Half of the land was owned by Myr, about a quarter by Arabs and the rest by the Israeli government.

But the former dovish government never got around to building Har Homa. On Wednesday, a ministerial committee headed by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu gave the green light to build, sparking international criticism and Palestinian outrage.
Abu Zayyad, who is also a Palestinian Authority legislator, said: "I wish he would win the case and stop the confiscation."
But he added he didn't think Middle East peace was what was uppermost in Myr's mind.
"He's a man who wants to make money," Abu Zayyad said.
Myr would not say how much he has invested over the years in planning for Har Homa which includes computer models and numerous scale models.

But he said the project once finished would bring $1.5 billion dollars in sales. Despite the vast sum, he differed with Abu Zayyad over his motivation for the project. He said he would be willing to put profits in a "humanitarian fund" as long as he got "replacement value for the land".
"It's not a question of money. It's a question of a life project," Myr said. "I love the hill."
